extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Latin literature / readers of Horace
extracted.subtask_description: Annotated text and commentary on Horace's Epistles (Book I) giving running translation, literary-critical notes, textual variants, and interpretive guidance on theme, style, and rhetorical devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme — simplicity and charm of country life
rubrics_metrics.description: The Epistle is a rhapsody upon the simplicity and charm of country life addressed to a cultivated man of the town.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose the epistle around a sustained contrast between rural and urban life, emphasizing contentment in the country and addressing it to an urban friend (e.g., Fuscus) to foreground the tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening style — conversational looseness and parentheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening paragraph (1-25) is loosely framed, with lengthy parentheses, giving an air of careless freedom of style, after the fashion of conversation in real life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use informal, parenthetical asides and a loose syntactic frame to create a conversational tone at the outset of an epistle; this helps simulate spoken intimacy and rhetorical spontaneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical device — fictional instructions as a framing ploy
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of writing a formal note to the Emperor to accompany the gift, Horace indulges in the fiction of sending a letter of instructions to the messenger, in which he humorously expresses his anxiety about the reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting work to an authority within a literary frame, consider indirect or fictionalized framing devices (e.g., 'instructions to a messenger') and self-deprecatory humor to defuse potential offence and dramatize the delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral/tonal stance — moderation and 'money should follow, not lead'
rubrics_metrics.description: Money stored up is for each his lord or his slave, but ought to follow, not lead, the twisted rope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate moderation and the primacy of virtuous self-control in tone and theme: wealth is to be subordinated, not the guiding principle of life. This moral stance recurs and shapes exempla and counsels in the epistles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of exempla and analogies to illustrate ethical lessons
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace uses comparisons and anecdotes (stag vs. horse, priest's runaway slave, the shoe analogy) to illustrate moral points about liberty, fortune, and fitting one's station.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ vivid analogies and brief anecdotes drawn from familiar rural or social life to make abstract moral claims concrete and memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailoring content to addressee — appeal to recipient's tastes
rubrics_metrics.description: Address specific friend and tailor content to their tastes (e.g., urbane Fuscus vs country lover), including local details and personalised contrasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select themes, examples, and tone that respond to the addressee's known preferences and status; personalised references increase rhetorical effectiveness and intimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural mix — blending personal news, moralizing, and practical instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Epistles combine personal news, moralizing reflections, occasional humorous episodes, and practical instructions (e.g., directions to a messenger), often closing with salutations or imperatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure an epistle to allow shifts between anecdote, ethical reflection, and concrete business; endings can revert to direct address or practical injunctions to ground the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly editorial practice — note variant readings and emendations
rubrics_metrics.description: The apparatus records variant manuscript readings, conjectural emendations (e.g., 'expellas early editions', 'VE: etc.'), and glosses; commentaries supply historical and philological notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In an annotated edition, document manuscript variants and editorial choices explicitly, explain conjectures, and provide philological, historical, or cultural glosses to justify readings and aid interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allusive density — classical references and learned allusions
rubrics_metrics.description: The letters freely allude to philosophical doctrines (Empedocles, Stoic rules), mythic/topical references (Dog-star, Lion, Phraates) and contemporary persons/events, presupposing an educated reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use erudite allusions and topical references to enrich argument and signal audience; supply notes where allusions might be obscure to readers to maintain clarity.
